title: Chip Industry Technical Paper Roundup: Oct. 20
gist: A weekly listing of seven new technical papers with no analysis: two use agentic AI in chip design (Argonne/UIUC on heterogeneous system design, Columbia/Google DeepMind on EDA verification infrastructure), and the others cover HBM2 power characterization (ETH Zurich/NYU), GAAFET leakage paths (Sandia), NEM-gated gain-cell eDRAM (UC Berkeley/Samsung/Intel), AI-accelerated 3D-IC thermal solving (Cadence/Notre Dame), and thermal side-channel attacks on autonomous vehicles (Missouri S&T). The signal comes from which institutions are working on what, not from any results, because the text reports none.

themes.theme: Agentic AI enters chip design and verification

insights.claim: Two of the seven papers in Semiconductor Engineering's Oct. 20 roundup use agentic AI for chip development: Argonne National Laboratory and UIUC apply it to heterogeneous system design across chip, scale-up, and scale-out domains, and Columbia University with Google DeepMind and Google argue for rethinking EDA infrastructure for agentic verification.
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
insights.so_what: Agentic EDA is moving past vendor marketing into national-lab and hyperscaler research, so incumbent EDA tool flows may need re-architecting for agents.
insights.quote: Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification

insights.claim: A Columbia University/Google DeepMind/Google paper is framed around rethinking EDA infrastructure for agentic systems in verification, which implies that current EDA tooling was not built for AI-agent users and is a bottleneck to automating RTL verification and debugging.
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
insights.so_what: Google's involvement suggests a hyperscaler push to make verification work with agents, which could pressure Cadence- and Synopsys-style tool interfaces.
insights.locator: Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA

insights.claim: ETH Zurich and NYU published an experimental analysis and model of power consumption in modern High Bandwidth Memory, built from measurements on real HBM2 DRAM chips rather than from vendor datasheet figures alone.
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
insights.so_what: HBM power is now a big enough constraint on AI accelerators that academics are measuring it on real silicon.
insights.quote: Understanding the Power Consumption of Modern High Bandwidth Memory: Experimental Analysis and Modeling Using Real HBM2 DRAM Chips

insights.claim: UC Berkeley, Samsung Electronics, and Intel jointly authored a paper on nanoelectromechanically gated gain-cell eDRAM, which the site's paper link describes as using nanoelectromechanical switches to make embedded DRAM more efficient.
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
insights.so_what: Two major chipmakers are co-researching gain-cell eDRAM, which points to interest in dense on-die memory alternatives to SRAM.
insights.quote: Nanoelectromechanical Switches Target More Efficient Embedded DRAM (UC Berkeley, Samsung, Intel)

insights.claim: Sandia National Laboratories and the Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology used predictive first-principles simulations to reveal new leakage paths in gate-all-around FETs (GAAFETs).
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
entities: Luxembourg Institute of Science and Technology
insights.so_what: Leakage mechanisms in GAA transistors are still being found, so there is ongoing reliability and power risk at the leading nodes.
insights.quote: Revealing New Leakage Paths in GAAFETs using Predictive First-Principles Simulations

insights.claim: Cadence Design Systems and the University of Notre Dame developed a composable, AI-accelerated iterative solver for thermal modeling of heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC packages.
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
insights.so_what: Thermal analysis is a gating problem for chiplet and 3D stacking, and Cadence is using AI acceleration to differentiate its multiphysics tools.
insights.quote: A Composable Thermal Solver For Heterogeneous 2.5D/3D-IC Packages (Cadence, Notre Dame)

insights.claim: A Missouri University of Science and Technology survey frames thermal side-channel and perception attacks as a new security risk category for autonomous vehicles.
insights.speaker: Linda Christensen
entities: Missouri University of Science and Technology
insights.so_what: AV security is widening from software and sensor spoofing to physical thermal attack vectors, which may add hardware-security requirements for automotive chips.
insights.quote: Thermal Side Channels Create New Security Risks For Autonomous Vehicles (Missouri S&T)

top_entities: Missouri University of Science and Technology
